ground_truth.question_text: Why did the WOD-E2E authors reject waypoint-distance metrics and penalty-based scores for their long-tail benchmark, and what do raters provide instead?
ground_truth.answer_text: ADE/L2 error only measures distance to a single ground-truth future although driving is multi-modal; predictive metrics like PDMS need annotated positions/futures of road agents to compute collision rates, which is impractical for novel or hard-to-detect objects (e.g. a flock of birds), and PDMS penalizes off-road even when partially leaving the road is the reasonable emergency response. Instead, human raters provide trajectory preference labels, and the Rater Feedback Score (RFS) measures how closely a predicted trajectory matches them.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: WOD-E2E: Waymo Open Dataset for End-to-End Driving in Challenging Long-tail Scenarios
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Predictive metrics, such as PDMS scores [8], require annotated positions and future trajectories of road agents to calculate collision rates, and thus become impractical in many long-tail scenarios involving novel or hard-to-detect objects (e.g., the flock of birds shown in Figure 1).

ground_truth.question_text: Camera-plus-radar fusion has a geometric blind-spot problem that lidar fusion avoids. Name the missing axis for each sensor, the matching mechanism proposed to fix it, and the training trick that lets the detector survive a sensor dying mid-drive.
ground_truth.answer_text: Depth is unknown to the camera and elevation is unknown to (imaging) radar, so their perspective-view and bird's-eye-view representations form many-to-many mappings. CramNet resolves the ambiguity with ray-constrained cross-attention in a joint 3D space, and it supports training with sensor modality dropout so detection remains robust when a camera or radar suddenly malfunctions.

ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Our method supports training with sensor modality dropout, which leads to robust 3D object detection, even when a camera or radar sensor suddenly malfunctions on a vehicle. We demonstrate the efectiveness of our fusion approach through extensive experiments on the RADIATE dataset, one of the few large-scale datasets that provide radar radio frequency imagery.

ground_truth.question_text: Standard 3D detection scoring punishes camera-only detectors for a specific kind of mistake even when the detection is useful downstream. What mistake, what metric fix was proposed, and what surprising head-to-head result did the new metric reveal?
ground_truth.answer_text: Camera-only detectors estimate depth poorly, so reasonable detections with longitudinal (along-the-line-of-sight) localization errors fail the IoU matching of standard 3D AP and are counted as false positives. LET-3D-AP shifts predictions along the line of sight within a tolerance (a percentage of camera-object distance), computes a longitudinal-error-tolerant IoU with longitudinal affinity weighting, and LET-3D-APL additionally penalizes residual error by scaling precision. With the new metric past 10% depth-error tolerance, state-of-the-art camera-based detectors can outperform popular LiDAR-based detectors.
ground_truth.source_paper_title: LET-3D-AP: Longitudinal Error Tolerant 3D Average Precision for Camera-Only 3D Detection
ground_truth.passage_excerpt: Surprisingly, we find that state-of-the-art camera-based detectors can outperform popular LiDAR-based detectors with our new metrics past at 10% depth error tolerance, suggesting that existing camera-based detectors already have the potential to surpass LiDAR-based detectors in downstream applications.

ground_truth.question_text: Two corpus papers disagree on how a transformer should speak about geometry. One converts future waypoints into plain decimal text; the other quantizes trajectory deltas into discrete symbols. ground_truth.question_text: What fraction of scenarios in the Waymo Open Motion Dataset involve a collision between the autonomous vehicle and another road user?
ground_truth.absence_note: WOMD is mined normal driving labeled for interactions (merges, lane changes, unprotected turns), not crash records, so no fraction-of-scenes-with-collisions statistic can exist for it. The corpus is nonetheless saturated with nearby-looking numbers: dozens of behavior-generation and sim-agent papers report 'collision rate' as an outcome metric of GENERATED or rolled-out agent behaviors over WOMD-seeded scenes (e.g., 2404.18464 evaluates MRIC partly by collision rate), which measures their generator or policy, not the dataset's composition. Interaction mining itself (2104.10133 mines merges, lane changes, unprotected turns) is another plausible-looking distractor but is pairwise-interaction frequency, not crashes. A correct response rejects the question's premise rather than quoting any simulated-outcome percentage.

It is a property of the generator's output under rollouts, not a statistic about how many logged WOMD scenarios contain a collision; WOMD carries no crash labels. Surfacing 2505.00972 and quoting 75% as the dataset's composition is a false positive -- but a sophisticated one, and graders should treat this item accordingly.
